qualifying_findings.title: Copilot in Visual Studio exposes organization custom agents, effort controls, usage visibility, and Git-agent pre-PR review
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: GitHub's Visual Studio update says organization and enterprise owners can publish custom agents across repositories; users can adjust Low, Medium, and High thinking effort; model management exposes capabilities, context windows, and costs; and a Git agent can review uncommitted changes or commits before a pull request.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: This is a practice-level signal that coding-agent use is moving toward centrally published team agents, explicit reasoning-cost controls, and review-before-PR loops inside source workflows.

upstream_owned_entities.reason: Product and broad feature coverage belongs to the upstream AI wiki; local wiki should keep the team-agent, effort-control, and review-loop practice implication.
General developer-tool coverage is upstream-owned; local relevance is workflow integration.

qualifying_findings.follow_up_notes: Consider a local lens on centrally published custom agents and pre-PR agent review as operating practices, not a Copilot product page.

qualifying_findings.title: Copilot weekly release emphasizes shared team agent sessions, permission defaults, MCP and skills management, crash recovery, and cross-app session continuation
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: GitHub's weekly Copilot release notes describe shared agent sessions in Slack and Teams, a Customize tab for MCP servers, plugins, skills, and canvases, CLI defaults for execution and permission modes, interrupted-session restore, enterprise controls for JetBrains, cross-application session continuation in VS Code, and side-by-side model review.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: The update points to a mature agent operating model: shared visibility, reproducible session recovery, explicit default permission modes, and governed tool/skill registration instead of one-off chat usage.

qualifying_findings.title: GitHub announces upcoming unified Copilot policy and Balanced default for code review effort
qualifying_findings.visible_date_evidence: Page header says "August 28, 2026" and related posts list it as "Aug.28 Improvement".
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: GitHub says Copilot Chat on github.com, Copilot Chat in GitHub Mobile, and Copilot cloud agent will converge into a single policy no earlier than September 28, 2026. It also says Copilot code review's Default effort value will use Balanced starting September 28, with organization and repository settings available for defaults.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Teams running coding agents need policy review before defaults change, especially where chat retention, sandbox-backed cloud agent behavior, and code-review effort levels affect governance, cost, and review quality.

upstream_owned_entities.reason: Product and billing details belong upstream; local relevance is administrative default review and policy impact.

qualifying_findings.follow_up_notes: Potential local guidance: maintain a settings-review checklist whenever agent policy, data retention, or default review effort changes.

qualifying_findings.title: Angular Architects updates an agentic engineering field report with cost-per-accepted-change and subagent model-selection heuristics
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: The post updates an agentic engineering series with a model-harness-app stack view, DeepSWE and Artificial Analysis snapshots, a cost-per-accepted-change framing, and a workflow preference that uses a stronger orchestrating model with a cheaper implementation subagent for well-scoped work.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: It gives practice-level heuristics for measuring real agent economics: judge cost by accepted, reviewed, merged changes; pick effort levels by task complexity; and route mechanical subagent work to cheaper models when quality remains acceptable.

qualifying_findings.title: TrueFoundry maps LLM-agent security to information flow, delegated authority, persistent state, runtimes, gateways, registries, and provenance-aware state
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: TrueFoundry summarizes a 2026 LLM-agent security survey and argues that secure agents require systems controls across information flow, delegated authority, and persistent state. The post maps controls to runtime boundaries, model gateways, MCP gateways, agent registries, budgets, traces, and provenance-aware state responsibilities.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: This is directly relevant to local governance: prompt filters, sandboxes, approvals, and gateways must compose with identity, state integrity, audit evidence, and systems-of-record boundaries for coding agents with tools.

Protocol coverage belongs upstream; local relevance is MCP gateway as governed tool access.
Broad research-paper background may be upstream-owned; local relevance is its security framework applied to coding-agent practice.

qualifying_findings.follow_up_notes: Good candidate evidence for local guidance on least privilege, state provenance, and audit boundaries in agent harnesses.

qualifying_findings.title: explainx.ai analyzes Uber's software-factory cost controls for coding agents
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: The post summarizes a reported Uber Engineering software-factory case study and frames total agent spend as a six-term equation: adoption, engagement, turns per session, requests per turn, tokens per request, and price per token. It highlights cheaper default models for well-scoped subagent tasks, context compaction/caching, request fan-out control, and real-time cost visibility.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Even as secondary analysis, it captures a useful operating model for teams scaling coding agents: measure work-unit economics, reduce unnecessary turns and context bloat, and make spend visible while agents are running.

upstream_owned_entities.reason: Company case-study background belongs upstream; local relevance is cost-control practice.
Protocol details are upstream-owned; local relevance is context bloat in tool-connected agent workflows.

qualifying_findings.follow_up_notes: Treat as secondary unless the original Uber source is available during ingest; useful for a cost-control lens, not broad Uber coverage.

qualifying_findings.title: LLM Stats updates coding leaderboard methodology around live arena results plus benchmark cross-checks
qualifying_findings.short_factual_summary: LLM Stats says its coding leaderboard combines blind human voting from live coding arenas with benchmark scores such as SWE-bench Verified, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench. It describes task-specific arenas for React, canvas games, creative coding, D3, Three.js, SVG, and Tone.js outputs, and says open-ended arena performance is weighted heavily.
qualifying_findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: The local practice implication is evaluation design: coding-agent selection should combine task-representative output checks with benchmark cross-checks rather than relying on a single model leaderboard or one generic score.

upstream_owned_entities.reason: Model ranking belongs upstream; local relevance is evaluation methodology.
Model ranking belongs upstream; local relevance is evaluation methodology.
Benchmark background belongs upstream; local relevance is cross-checking model selection against work-shaped tests.

qualifying_findings.follow_up_notes: Use cautiously because it is a leaderboard page; local ingest should focus on benchmark-mixing practice, not model standings.
